notes.h: Rural housing in the nineteenth century (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Early nineteenth-century housing in Ireland reflected the materials available locally and the wealth of each household.
points: Labourers and small farmers lived in single-storey thatched cottages with stone or mud walls, a half-door and a small number of windows.
Thatch was made of reeds, straw or hay, and an open hearth in the main room was used for both cooking and heating.
Some cottages had a loft directly under the thatch, reached by a ladder, where children slept.
Prosperous farmers lived in two-storey, slate-roofed houses with several bedrooms and a parlour.
Wealthy landowners lived in large estate houses, with servants' quarters generally in the basement.
Diagram: a thatched cottage in cross-section, showing the thatched roof, the loft reached by ladder, the open hearth and the half-door.

notes.h: Urban and late nineteenth-century housing (Higher Level only)
points: Georgian terraces in towns were two, three or four storeys high, with basements and high ceilings.
Workers lived in small single-storey cottages or in crowded tenements, and shopkeepers often lived above their shops.
Improved transport in the later nineteenth century brought a greater variety of building materials, and houses became more ornate in Gothic and Tudor styles.
Two-storey, slate-roofed stone buildings became the most common rural dwelling by the end of the century.
As wealthier families moved to suburban terraced houses, many large Georgian houses in towns were divided and rented to poorer families.

notes.h: Housing in the early twentieth century (Higher Level only)
points: Detached and semi-detached houses appeared, along with council housing and new housing estates.
Brick with plaster walls replaced stone, and tiles replaced slates; two-storey houses were built where land was expensive.
Rural electrification in the 1950s changed rural homes, and government housing grants funded improvements to rural houses.
The slate-roofed bungalow gradually replaced the thatched cottage in rural Ireland.

notes.h: Housing in the late twentieth and twenty-first centuries (Higher Level only)
points: Late twentieth-century private estates were built to a common design, while individual private houses varied between classical and modern styles.
Building regulations greatly improved housing standards, and new materials such as double glazing, PVC and fibreglass came into use.
Twenty-first-century estates usually consist of one style but include single-storey detached, dormer and two-storey semi-detached houses.
Old dilapidated buildings and thatched cottages are restored, and custom-designed houses are built on private sites.
Attic space is converted into rooms with Velux roof windows, and conservatories and sunroom extensions are added to many houses.

notes.h: Popular housing styles in Ireland today
points: Bungalows are single-storey and suit older people and rural sites; the dormer bungalow adds rooms in the roof space.
Two-storey detached houses suit large families and sites with space for a garden.
Semi-detached and terraced houses make efficient use of land; a terraced house loses less heat than a detached house because it shares walls with its neighbours.
Apartments save space and maintenance, suit first-time buyers, downsizers and city living, and are usually in secure complexes.
Townhouses are multi-storey homes built on small urban sites, with limited outdoor space.
Traditional, neo-Georgian and restored houses offer proportion and character, while modern minimalist homes are bright and easy to care for.
Old cottages are kept for holiday and local use in tourist areas.

notes.h: Factors influencing the choice of housing style
points: Social factors: family size, children's ages, special needs or disability, and whether the household wants a garden or office space.
Cultural factors: personal taste and aesthetics, and regional building traditions such as local stone or slate that shape the look of rural houses.
Economic factors: income and money available, the cost of land, and the resale value and investment potential of the style.
Environmental factors: aspect, so that south-facing rooms gain daylight and solar heat; exposure to wind and rain; and energy efficiency through insulation and glazing.
Environmental factors: the style must fit the surrounding landscape and neighbouring buildings, and planning rules control scale and materials in many areas.
Setting: a school visit to houses from different periods, or photographs of house styles used to discuss their suitability to their surroundings.

keyTerms.definition: A roof covering of reeds, straw or hay, used on rural cottages in nineteenth-century Ireland.
A door divided horizontally so that the top half can be opened separately, common on rural cottages.
A row of town houses of two to four storeys, with basements and high ceilings, built in Irish towns in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.
A large house or building divided into rooms or flats, each let to a separate family, common in Irish towns in the nineteenth century.
The extension of mains electricity to rural homes, which in Ireland was carried out mainly in the 1950s.
A single-storey house with rooms built into the roof space behind dormer windows.
The direction a house or room faces, which determines how much daylight and solar heat it receives.
A modern style that uses the proportions and symmetry of Georgian houses in new construction.
The repair of an older building to its original character, often supported by grants for listed or traditional buildings.

factCards.term: Three features of a nineteenth-century rural cottage
factCards.definition: Single-storey construction; a thatched roof; an open hearth used for cooking and heating.

factCards.term: Four categories of factors influencing housing style
factCards.definition: Social, cultural, economic and environmental factors.

factCards.term: Two causes of change in rural housing in the mid-twentieth century
factCards.definition: Rural electrification and government housing grants.

factCards.term: Late nineteenth-century use of Georgian town houses
factCards.definition: They were divided and let to poorer families as wealthier residents moved to suburban terraced houses.

factCards.term: Three benefits of a bungalow for older people
factCards.definition: No stairs to climb; step-free access that is easier to adapt; a compact layout that is simpler to heat and maintain.

factCards.term: Two features of a Georgian town house
factCards.definition: Two to four storeys with basements; high ceilings and prominent doorways.

questions.prompt: Describe the main features of a typical rural house in Ireland in the early nineteenth century.
questions.model: Single-storey thatched cottage with stone or mud walls and few windows; a half-door; an open hearth used for cooking and heating; a loft under the thatch reached by a ladder, where children slept. Wealthier farmers had two-storey slated houses; landowners had estate houses.

questions.prompt: Explain how social and economic factors influence a household's choice between a bungalow, a semi-detached house and an apartment.
questions.model: Social factors: family size and the number of bedrooms needed; children's ages and the need for a garden; older people or people with a disability may need a single-storey bungalow or step-free access; a single person or couple may prefer an apartment near work, amenities and transport; privacy and the wish to live close to neighbours. Economic factors: income and the money available for a deposit or building; the cost of land, which pushes urban development towards apartments and two-storey houses; running costs, with terraced and semi-detached houses cheaper to heat than detached ones; resale value and investment potential of the chosen style. Each factor should be linked to the specific style: the bungalow suits older people on a larger rural site, the semi-detached house suits a growing family in a suburb, and the apartment suits first-time buyers and downsizers in a city.
